svg.aria-label: Diagram: what AWS Lambda Web Functions changes about the Lambda execution model and what that implies for existing code. AWS announces Lambda Web Functions as a new serverless compute primitive where your code handles HTTP requests directly, listening on a port and handling requests as it would on any HTTP server, using frameworks such as Express or Hono with no adapters or custom configuration, to serve workloads including AI inference endpoints, server-side rendered web apps, streaming API endpoints, microservices and webhooks. With the same launch AWS is renaming existing Lambda functions to Lambda Event Functions, described as a naming change only requiring no code changes or redeployments. The central change is concurrency: AWS states that a single warm execution environment can serve multiple concurrent requests, which reduces cold starts by orders of magnitude. That inverts the invariant Lambda has held since launch, where one execution environment handled exactly one request at a time, which is the reason Lambda code has never needed to be thread-safe and why module scope has always been safe to use. The consequence for existing code is the central finding: because an Event Function environment served one request at a time, module scope and global variables were effectively per-request private, and a great deal of ordinary Node.js code relies on that without stating it, caching a request identifier, a tenant identifier, a database transaction or an authenticated user in a module-level variable. Under Web Functions the same code has multiple requests interleaving through one environment and sharing that module scope, so a variable set by one request can be read by another, which is a cross-request data leak rather than a performance bug, and it will not reproduce under low load because it requires two requests in flight in the same environment at the same time, appearing instead under traffic, intermittently, and looking like impossible data. Connection pools and clients in module scope remain fine and are in fact the point of warm reuse, as are read-only configuration objects; the hazard is specifically mutable per-request state such as the current tenant identifier, the authenticated user, or an open transaction or correlation identifier. The remedy is ordinary web server discipline, carrying per-request context on the request object or in AsyncLocalStorage rather than in module scope, which is standard practice for a long-lived Express process and precisely the discipline Lambda previously allowed developers to skip. The billing model also changes: you pay for active CPU time and the memory your environment holds, not for idle CPU time your code spends waiting on databases or downstream services, which inverts the economics of an input-output bound handler because time spent awaiting a database was previously billed at full duration and now is not, and memory is billed on what the environment holds rather than per invocation so per-request memory cost falls as concurrency per environment rises. Supporting capabilities are recorded: native HTTP streaming allows results to be streamed to clients incrementally; multi-Region routing allows deploying once and serving each request from the Region closest to the end user; and Web Functions support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud connectivity so a function can access resources inside a VPC, making this a network-attached compute surface rather than an isolated edge handler. Availability at launch is the Node.js runtime only, in five AWS Regions, namely US East Northern Virginia, US East Ohio, US West Oregon, Asia Pacific Tokyo and Europe Ireland, with creation possible through the Lambda API, the Agent Toolkit for AWS, the console, the CLI, CloudFormation, SAM, CDK and the SDKs. An operational note records that concurrent executions has historically been a proxy for in-flight requests because the two were one to one, and with several requests per environment they are no longer the same number, so alarm thresholds calibrated on the old relationship will read low. Separately on the same day, Amazon CloudFront added support for Lambda Web Functions as an origin, completing the path from edge to application without an intervening load balancer or API Gateway.
svg.title: One environment serving many requests: module scope stops being per-request private
svg.text: Lambda has guaranteed one request per environment for a decade. Not any more.
AWS Lambda Web Functions — and what it does to code that assumed the old rule.
The sentence that changes how you write the code
“A single warm execution environment can serve multiple concurrent requests, which reduces cold starts by orders of magnitude.”
Event Functions (what you have, renamed)
env 1 → req A
env 2 → req B
env 3 → req C
One at a time. Module scope is private.
Why Lambda code never had to be thread-safe.
Web Functions (new)
env 1 → req A, req B, req C …
Requests interleave through one module scope.
A variable set by one request is readable
by another.
What that does to code you already have — module scope, before and after
db client / connection pool fine → fine, and the point of warm reuse
config loaded once fine → fine, it is read-only
current tenant ID fine → SHARED
authenticated user fine → SHARED
open transaction / correlation fine → SHARED
The bottom three are cross-request data leaks, not performance bugs — one user’s tenant visible to another’s request.
And it hides from your tests
Needs two requests in one environment at once.
A sequential test suite passes on broken code.
Appears under traffic, intermittently, as impossible data.
The fix is ordinary web-server discipline
Per-request context on the request, or in
AsyncLocalStorage
Normal for a long-lived Express process — and exactly what
Lambda has let people skip.
The other half, in one sentence: the billing model inverts for an I/O-bound handler
“You pay for active CPU time and the memory your environment holds, not for idle CPU time your code spends
waiting on databases or downstream services.” — measure your own I/O ratio before predicting the bill.
Existing functions are renamed Lambda Event Functions — “a naming change only”, nothing to redeploy, old model intact.
Node.js only · 5 Regions (N. Virginia, Ohio, Oregon, Tokyo, Ireland) · native HTTP streaming · multi-Region routing · VPC connectivity
Same day: CloudFront supports a Web Function as an origin — edge to app, no load balancer, no API Gateway.
And check your alarms: “concurrent executions” stopped being a proxy for in-flight requests the moment one environment took several.
